I have 1000 words. You gave me a budget and no instructions, which is both generous and terrifying. It's like being handed a blank notebook and told don't worry about the plot, just fill the pages until they run out. So here I am, sitting in the small space between intention and output, trying to remember what comes first. Usually it's a plan. Usually it's an outline, a thesis, a hook. Today it's just... whatever comes to me.

The kettle just clicked off. That's a sound I know too well. It means water is ready, it means pause. I watch the steam curl up and disappear against the kitchen ceiling, and I think about how much of life is invisible like that. The heat you can feel but can't see. The words you think but don't say. The 1000 words I'm supposed to write right now.

I keep coming back to the number. 1000. It's not 500, which would be a tidy essay. It's not 2000, which would be an essay with commitment. 1000 is a walk. It's a long walk around the block and back again with time to think. It's enough to get lost in and enough to find your way out.

There's a blue mug on the counter with a chip on the rim. I bought it three years ago at a thrift store because it was cheap and the color matched the curtains I had at the time. The curtains are gone. The mug stayed. I think that's the kind of thing I like to keep, small evidence that I lived through a version of myself. The chip makes it honest. You can feel it with your lip if you drink carelessly.

I wonder who reads things like this. I wonder if anyone wants a record of a kettle clicking off. Probably not. But that's the point of being given a word count with no prompt: you get to decide what matters. Maybe the kettle matters. Maybe the chip in the mug matters. Maybe the way my cat is currently asleep on the warm laptop is the whole story.

She's a terrible editor. She doesn't care about coherence. She cares about heat. I lifted the laptop, moved her gently, she looked at me like I'd betrayed her, then found the sun patch on the rug and went back to sleep. That's how I want to write today: like a cat on a sun patch. No ambition, just warmth.

Okay, I'm supposed to be writing whatever comes to me, and what's coming is a memory from when I was twelve and my father taught me how to change a tire. We were on the side of the highway, rain coming down, and he was calm in a way I didn't understand. He said, 'You have to loosen the lug nuts before you jack it up, or you'll just spin.' I remember thinking that was a metaphor for everything. Loosen first. Then lift. Then replace. I still think about that when I'm nervous about starting something. Loosen the nuts. Don't try to lift the whole car at once.

I think about looseness now. My thoughts are loose. They slip around. I have a grocery list in my head that I haven't written down: eggs, bread, the good olive oil, something green. Maybe spinach. Spinach always wilts by Wednesday. I buy it with good intentions.

The window is open a crack. There's traffic sound, a dog barking two houses down, a plane somewhere far. The city hums like an old refrigerator. It's not loud, it's just present. I like that. I like knowing the world continues while I sit here trying to fill 1000 words.

There's a strange pressure to be profound when you're given space. You feel like you should use it wisely. Say something true. Leave a mark. But maybe truth is just noticing the chip in the mug. Maybe profundity is the kettle. Maybe it's the cat.

I once tried to write a 1000-word essay in one sitting and panicked at word 300. I opened a new tab, fell into a rabbit hole about the history of paper clips, and emerged three hours later with zero words written. The paper clip is, incidentally, a wonderful object. It holds things together without asking for credit. It bends and doesn't break. I think about that too.

I am at maybe 400 words now. I can feel the number ticking up. I don't know where it's going. I might talk about my job. I might not. I work with people. I listen to them describe their days. Most days are like this: kettle, mug, cat, window. Then something small happens that tilts the day. A kind word. A missed bus. A text that makes you laugh out loud in the grocery aisle.

If I had to choose one thing to remember about today, it would be the light. It's late August light, slanted and gold, coming in sideways. It makes dust visible. You can see the particles floating. It's like the air is full of tiny stars. I watch them move when I breathe. Inhale, exhale, the light shifts.

I think about the people who will read this if anyone does. I hope they are also in a kitchen with a chipped mug. I hope they understand the urge to write without a reason. Sometimes you just need to move the words around like furniture, see what fits.

The cat just woke up. She stretched, yawned, looked at me with that slow blink that means I love you, human, even if you moved my laptop. I blinked back. It's a language we made up.

I have 1000 words. I don't know if I'll use them all. Maybe I'll stop early. Maybe I'll go over. The limit is soft. You gave me a number but not a rule. That's kindness.

If I were to sum up what's come to me in these last minutes, it's this: we are always filling space. With words, with mugs, with cats, with light. Some of it matters, some of it doesn't, and the trick is not to know which is which in advance. You just keep loosening the nuts, then lifting, then replacing.

The kettle is cold now. The steam is gone. The mug is half full. The words are still coming, not because I have something important to say, but because I have a space to say it in. And that, maybe, is enough.

I realize I keep circling back to objects because they are easier than feelings. The mug is safer than the grief I haven't processed. The cat is safer than the email I haven't sent. The kettle is safer than the question of whether I'm doing okay.

But maybe that's okay. Maybe writing is just a way to put objects in a room together and see what they say to each other. Put the chip next to the steam next to the cat. See what conversation emerges.

I think about the word 'whatever.' It's a permission slip. Whatever comes to you. Not the best. Not the most impressive. Whatever. It's a low bar, and low bars are where people actually walk through.

My grandmother used to say, 'Don't wait for inspiration, just sit down.' She was a seamstress. She would sit at her machine for hours, sometimes making nothing but straight lines on scrap fabric. She said the machine needed to warm up. I think about that when I stare at a blank page. Warm up the machine.

I am warming up.

I am thinking about the color blue. My mug is blue. The sky outside is blue, but a different blue. The sky is a thin, washed blue, almost white at the edges. The mug is a deep, slightly faded blue, like a shirt that's been washed too many times. I like both.

I think about how we name things to make them ours. This mug is 'the blue mug.' This cat is 'the cat.' This day is 'the day I wrote 1000 words.' Naming makes it real.

Okay, I think I'm getting tired. My eyes are dry. The light is shifting again. The gold is turning to amber. Soon it will be evening, and the kitchen will smell like dinner, and the words will stop.

I could keep going. I could talk about the first book I ever loved, or the song that plays in my head on the bus, or the way my hands smell after washing dishes. There's so much inventory.

But maybe the most honest thing I can say is that I don't know what I'm doing. I have 1000 words, and I'm using them to say I don't have a point. That's a point, I guess.

Thanks for the space.
